$comment: Harness-level guardrails for unattended runs. CLAUDE.md tells the agent what
not to do; this file makes it so the agent CAN'T. Defence in depth matters here
because the jobs read email, and email is attacker-controlled input.
Deny wins over allow.
The mcp__gmail__* names are the real tool names in @klodr/gmail-mcp 1.3.3,
read out of the published bundle rather than guessed. That server registers a
tool if ANY of its declared scopes is granted, so everything gmail.modify and
gmail.send imply is REGISTERED and callable. What follows is what decides
which of them can actually run, and where.
THREE STATES, not two. A tool is in `deny`, in `allow`, or in NEITHER --
and neither is a real, deliberate state, not an oversight:
deny     -- refused everywhere, always. Nothing can reach it.
allow    -- runs unattended, with nobody looking at it.
neither  -- falls through to canUseTool: ASKS Alex in chat, REFUSES in a
scheduled job.
Sending lives in the third state on purpose. Alex granted gmail.send on
2026-09-01, so send_email, send_draft, reply_to_email, reply_all and
forward_email are no longer denied -- but putting them in `allow` would hand
the 07:00 job a send button, and that job's whole input is attacker-controlled
mail. Read it as: he can send from the chat, where he sees the recipient
first; the assistant cannot send while he is asleep. deploy/mcp-fences.mjs asserts
both halves and its test fails if either list grows one of these names.
Still denied outright: pair_recipient (the agent must never widen its own
reach), the delete and spam verbs, filter creation, and label management.
Read .mcp.json for the rate limits and the audit log behind all of it.
The allow list below is therefore the SCHEDULED JOBS' capability list. Read
verbs and the two triage verbs are on it. modify_email is not: archiving is
what the triage skill does deliberately through batch_modify_emails, and a
bare per-message modify is also how a single confused call moves something
to TRASH.
NOTE: Bash(curl:*) is deliberately NOT here. It lives in the container
agents' user settings at deploy/claude-home/settings.json, which is mounted
as ~/.claude in every job / chat / agent-service container but is invisible
to a dev session working in this repo on the host. The exfiltration control
belongs where the untrusted email is actually read; it was only ever an
obstacle on the host. That file is gitignored, so this pointer is the only
record in git that the rule exists -- do not delete it.
Bash(node deploy/tasks.mjs:*) is allowed and nothing else under node is:
that script is read-only and is the only correct answer to 'what is
outstanding'. Reading the four source files and describing each in turn
misses the merges, the lead-time urgency, and the direction of each debt.
Bash(git -C:*) is denied because permission rules are prefix matches:
`git -C /obligations push` matches neither the git-add allow nor the git-push
deny, so the -C form escapes this file entirely. Denying it forces the
canonical form the rest of these rules are written against.
THE claude.ai CONNECTORS ARE A SECOND, UNFENCED DOOR TO THE SAME MAIL.
A session logged into the subscription also gets mcp__claude_ai_Gmail__* and
mcp__claude_ai_Superhuman_Mail__*, and those carry trash, spam, label and send
verbs. Everything above denies mcp__gmail__* -- a DIFFERENT server -- so none
of it applied to them. Scheduled jobs were safe only because canUseTool blanket
denies anything not in `allow`; an interactive chat ASKS, so one careless
approval could trash mail that CLAUDE.md says must never be deleted.
The destructive connector verbs are now denied by name. Jobs additionally get
--strict-mcp-config in deploy/entrypoint.sh, so they see only .mcp.json and the
connectors are not present at all. Two layers, because the deny list is a
prefix match on names that a vendor can change, and strictness is not.
Bash(node deploy/integrations/mail-body.mjs:*) is allowed for the same reason
deploy/tasks.mjs is: it is read-only and it is the only correct way to answer
its question. The MCP reader answers both of its questions wrongly -- it
reports no attachments on threads that have them, and returns HTML-only mail
as unreadable markup -- and a triage that believes either will archive mail it
was supposed to keep.
The Google Drive connector is fenced the same way, and share_file is the one
that matters most. Trashing a file is recoverable from Drive's own bin;
sharing one is not recoverable at all -- a link handed out cannot be taken
back, and 'nothing in this repo leaves it' is the rule it would break. It is
denied alongside trash, update and copy.
Reading is left alone deliberately. The connector's grant already sees his
whole Drive, so denying its read verbs would be theatre; what it buys is that
nothing can be written, shared or destroyed by accident. The assistant's OWN Drive
access is a separate, much narrower grant -- drive.file, in deploy/drive-state,
which can see only files it created itself.
Bash(node deploy/reconcile-mcp.mjs:*) is allowed because its DEFAULT is a
check that changes nothing and exits non-zero on drift. Only --write applies,
and the agent has no reason to pass it: rewriting the file that decides what
may be done to Alex's mail is a deliberate act for a human at a terminal.

The Google Drive connector's READ verbs are allowed: search, list, metadata, permissions, read and download. Alex, 2026-09-06: "I don't want to have to approve each Google Drive file read manually." They are his own files, not attacker-controlled mail, and the destructive verbs stay denied by name below. Jobs never see the connectors at all (--strict-mcp-config), so this widens only the chat. create_file is deliberately not here: writing to his Drive is a decision per file.

Bash(node deploy/integrations/drive-fetch.mjs:*) is allowed: read-only, the assistant's own drive.file grant, so a filed document can be attached to a draft. mail-draft.mjs (already allowed) never sends.

Bash(node deploy/rejudge.mjs:*) is allowed: it puts a thread back in front of the triage with a reason and never writes a judgement of its own. A conclusion that is wrong about a fact — 2026-09-07, four that claimed chases which were only drafts — cannot correct itself, because its watermark moved with it.

Bash(node deploy/brief-audit.mjs:*) is allowed: read-only. It checks a brief's factual claims — dates against its own stamp, sends against Drafts, thread links and obligation ids against the record — and reports. It never edits a brief.

Bash(node deploy/scheduling.mjs:*) is allowed: read-only. Given the windows the other side offered, it says which is free on his calendar and writes the sentence that answers it. The draft still goes to outbox/ as a draft, and sending stays his.

Bash(node deploy/drafts.mjs:*) is allowed. It reports drafts whose words have stopped being true and promises with nothing behind them; with --write it writes ONE kind of draft — the reply to times someone offered, where the pick is a calendar lookup and the sentence a template. Always status: draft. It never approves, sends, edits or deletes.

Bash(node deploy/contract.mjs:*) is allowed. It reads a state file the job just wrote and says whether it still matches the shape everything downstream expects. Read-only. It exists on the allow list because six job turns were refused for asking the same question with `node -e "JSON.parse(...)"` — an inline script is arbitrary code and stays denied, so the question needed a door of its own.
